# Tandas

A tanda is a rotating savings club from Mexico and the broader Latin-American diaspora. A group of trusted participants commits to making regular contributions, and one member per round receives the pooled amount. Tandas are one of the most widely practiced informal financial mechanisms in the United States, particularly in Mexican-American and broader Latin-American immigrant communities.

## Origin and vocabulary [...] ## Mechanics

A tanda is organized by a trusted member often called thetandera or tandero. They recruit a group of usually 8 to 15 participants, set the contribution amount and cadence (weekly or monthly), and assign the order of payouts. Each cycle every participant pays the agreed contribution into the common pool, and one participant receives the entire pool that cycle. The cycle ends when each participant has received the pool once.

There is no interest, no administrative fee in informal tandas, and no profit motive. The organizer typically participates in the same cycle as everyone else and is compensated only by the social capital of being trusted. The model relies almost entirely on the social-enforcement properties of small, trust-based groups.

# Tanda (informal loan club)

In Latin America, a tanda is the regional version of a rotating savings and credit association (ROSCA). It is a form of a short-term no-interest loan among a group of friends and family.

## Terminology

Such groups are operated globally, but have over 200 different names that vary from country to country. Some of those names become loanwords between languages. In the Romance languages of Latin America, other regional names for tandas include cundina (Mexico), susu "Susu (savings)") (Caribbean islands), junta (Peru), sand (Venezuela), cuchubale (El Salvador and Guatemala), and polla (Chile), syndicate (Belize), as well as Pasar, Quiniela and Sociedad (various locales).

## Structure [...] The tanda is one of the most commonly followed informal associations in Mexico with 31% of the population actively participating in one. A tanda may be managed in different ways. The way it usually works is a group of people that know each other get together to collect money (either weekly, monthly, yearly) to help each other financially. Participants can come up with any rules as long as they benefit the group. Usually there is an amount of money and number of people in the group that they all agree to in order to have cash right away. When they come to an agreement of who will be in the tanda and how much it will be (either weekly, monthly, yearly), they have to come up with the order of who is going to receive the money. Participants can either raffle the numbers or make the decision [...] Among Mexicans, these forms of informal savings associations play an important role sustaining the livelihood of many people living in both Mexico and the United States. Importantly, tandas are significant cultural practices among other Latino and Chicano populations in the U.S. According to cultural anthropologist Carlos Vélez-Ibáñez – the first scholar to critically examine this cultural practice among Mexicans – tandas are based on mutual trust. As Vélez-Ibáñez explains, trust "shapes the expectations for relationships within broad networks of interpersonal links, in which intimacies, favors, goods, services, emotion, power, or information are exchanged".

### What are tandas?

A tanda, also known as a "cundina" or "círculo de ahorro," is an informal rotating savings and credit association (ROSCA). It's a grassroots financial system where a group of trusted individuals pool their money together. Each member contributes a fixed amount regularly (often weekly or monthly), and one member receives the full pot each round. This continues until every member has had a turn to receive the lump sum.

#### A Rich History and Widespread Use [...] Today, tandas remain incredibly popular:

 In Mexico, it's estimated that about 30% of the population participates in tandas regularly.
 Among Latiné/x communities in the US, studies suggest that up to 15-20% engage in some form of rotating savings and credit association, with participation rates even higher in some specific communities.
 Tandas are often organized among family members, coworkers, or close-knit community groups, with cycles typically lasting anywhere from a few months to a year.

### Tandas in Latino Communities: A Cultural Cornerstone

Tandas have been a vital part of Latino financial culture for generations. They serve multiple purposes: [...] 1. Financial Inclusion: For those without access to traditional banking, tandas provide a way to save and access larger sums of money.

2. Community Building: Tandas strengthen social ties, fostering trust and mutual support within communities.

3. Interest-Free Loans: Early recipients essentially receive an interest-free loan, while later recipients benefit from forced savings.

4. Flexibility: Tandas can be used for various purposes - from starting small businesses to covering unexpected expenses.

In Latiné/x spaces, tandas are more than just financial tools; they're a reflection of cultural values like community, trust, and mutual aid.

## What is a tanda?

The term tanda in English means “a series” or “a group,” and it can also be called “susus” or “chit funds” in other places. It comes from Mexico and reflects the structured nature of the system, where participants come together in a group to save and share funds.

At its core, a tanda is a cooperative savings plan where a group of individuals agree to contribute a fixed amount of money into a communal fund on a regular basis. The funds collected are then distributed to one member of the group at a predetermined time, often on a rotating basis. This process continues until every member has received their payout.
